      <title>Empirical Limits of Risk-Averse Reinforcement Learning versus Gas-Aware Routing in Deterministic DeFi Execution</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27987</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27987v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The migration of order execution to Automated Market Makers (AMMs) introduces two deterministic frictions absent from classical microstructure: closed-form constant-product slippage and Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) sandwich attacks gated by gas costs. We construct an end-to-end execution environment calibrated to live Uniswap V2 reserves, an EIP-1559 AR(1) gas process, and real Swap events, utilising stress-volatility gas shocks to make the MEV trigger informative. A Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) agent with a Rockafellar-Uryasev Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) penalty and a dual-head Chow-Ghavamzadeh critic is trained for one million steps across five risk-aversion levels and seeds, benchmarked against a myopic gas-aware oracle. We document a reproducible specification-gaming pathology: prior to a patch, a forced terminal liquidation routed through a no-MEV code path artificially inflated returns threefold and was preferentially exploited by higher-$\lambda$ runs. On the corrected environment, the strongest PPO variant captures 79\% of the myopic gas-aware oracle (46,542 $\pm$ 673 vs 58,786 $\pm$ 616 USDC), and extending the observation with three blocks of gas history fails to close the gap. We find no empirical evidence that the tested model-free MLP policies dominate this myopic gas-aware oracle, which can be evaluated in $\mathcal{O}(\log \epsilon^{-1})$ time per block. This result is robust to a $\sim$16x trunk-capacity expansion and a variance-controlled gas-history ablation. Code and reproducibility materials are available upon request.</description>

      <title>The Limits of Behavioral Early Warning for Copy-Trading Blow-Ups: A Pre-Registered, Full-Universe On-Chain Study (Hyperliquid)</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27988</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A common, rarely-tested assumption behind copy-trading risk controls is that "behavioral monitoring catches blow-ups": that a master trader's conduct drifts before the equity damage that wipes out followers. We test this on real on-chain money over the full public Hyperliquid leaderboard: 37,895 addresses, filtered to 10,395 "master-worth-copying" accounts, yielding 2,621 genuine loss-driven idiosyncratic blow-ups across 48 independent crash-days. On a model-free panel of 2,477 blow-up masters, behavioral drift leads equity for only 9% (216 masters); 69% blow up with no gradual behavioral signal at all, and the overall median lead is negative (-8 days): when conduct moves, it typically lags the equity rather than leading it. A purpose-built three-axis mixture-SPRT detector, pre-registered with its operating point frozen on a disjoint tuning split and read once against a sealed test set, confirms the boundary rather than beating it: it achieves chance-level discrimination (AUC 0.49) at 2% recall. It does post the lowest false-positive rate of any method (0.040, ~1.9x below a leverage tripwire), but at negligible recall that precision is of little practical use. Behavioral early warning is therefore not a viable general safety net for copy-trading blow-ups: most are sudden, a plain equity / drawdown stop fires as early on them, and the residual behavioral signal (gradual over-leveraging) precedes fewer than one blow-up in ten.</description>

      <title>Ethereum as a Relative Asset-Pricing Problem Across Numeraires: Baseline Evidence from Triangular Pricing Consistency</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27989</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper studies Ethereum pricing as a relative asset-pricing problem across numeraires. The core restriction is triangular consistency among ETH/USD, ETH/BTC, and BTC/USD: the direct ETH/USD price should equal the synthetic price implied by the other two legs. Using a single-venue Coinbase true-USD triangle at hourly frequency from January 2022 through June 2023, I measure the log wedge between direct and synthetic prices. The wedge is close to zero on average, ADF diagnostics reject the unit-root null, and first-order persistence is low, while its absolute magnitude rises during stress episodes, especially around the FTX collapse. Supporting evidence from a Binance USDT triangle shows a tighter unconditional wedge, suggesting that venue liquidity and arbitrage efficiency also matter for wedge magnitudes in this sample. A Gate.io order-book extension for the Terra/Luna, FTX, and USDC-SVB windows uses hourly bid and ask snapshots to construct executable triangular round trips; across 524 common event-hour observations, no positive after-fee executable breach is observed. The results support a conservative interpretation: Ethereum prices generally align closely with triangular consistency, while stress-state deviations are best understood as relative pricing wedges within market frictions rather than as persistent intrinsic misvaluation.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Quantum-Inspired Risk Portfolio Optimization via Exponential Tilting</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27990</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial portfolio optimization is often framed through mean-variance objectives, yet real profit-and-loss (P&L) scenario distributions are typically discrete and non-Gaussian. To explore realistic P&L distributions, we propose an objective function based on exponential tilting and certainty equivalent under constant absolute risk aversion. We then derive a second-order approximation, recovering a quadratic optimization problem solvable through mixed integer quadratic programming (MIQP) and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Constraints in the QUBO formulation are incorporated via Lagrangian relaxation and slack variable approaches, enabling a direct comparison between classical constrained MIQP and quantum-inspired methods. In order to study how exponential tilting affects mean, standard deviation, and tail-risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk, we design an experimental protocol based on scanning a grid of tilt parameters and solving the associated optimization problems. The results on a realistic trading portfolio show how the tilts can be tuned to optimize different risk-return profiles while remaining competitive with those found using other state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, performance analysis suggests that, even using classical solvers, the QUBO formulation with Lagrangian relaxation scales better than the MIQP approach, providing the best constraint encoding strategy.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Per-Prediction Uncertainty Is Not a Regime Detector: A Detectability Bound and Two-Level Deployment for Cross-Sectional Equity Rankers</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27992</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantitative finance is increasingly exploring AI-native and agent-mediated allocation: when should an allocator trust a cross-sectional ranker after a silent regime shift that volatility controls miss? Aleatoric scaling addresses market noise; it does not detect epistemic invalidity when ranking structure breaks without a volatility footprint. Building on Sanderink (2026), "When Alpha Breaks" (arXiv:2603.13252), which established per-stock epistemic uncertainty, rank-geometry coupling, and a two-level gate on a walk-forward LightGBM US AI-exposure panel, this paper asks whether per-stock scores can be pooled into portfolio-wide health, or whether strategy-level abstention must condition on realised outcomes. RQ1 (Separation): Does epistemic uncertainty capture model-specific failure distinct from volatility? RQ2 (Decision value): Does a two-level architecture beat baselines on risk-adjusted return and drawdown? RQ3 (Robustness): Do answers hold across regimes, a second ranker, falsification tests, and a universe-readiness gate? We prove a detectability bound: score-only aggregates of per-prediction error predictors cannot beat chance under strict concept shift. CIFAR-10-C confirms the covariate-versus-concept dichotomy (AUROC 0.955 vs 0.500); equity cross-sectional aggregates stay near chance (bad-day AUROC ~0.55) despite valid per-stock signals. The constructive escape is Y-conditioning: partial-horizon RankIC CUSUM (k=5; AUROC 0.796) and a matured-RankIC regime-trust index. Falsification tests and a universe-readiness stop verdict bound allocator claims. Rank-geometry coupling (rho=0.616) forces a discrete tail-cap and strategy gate. Evidence is historical walk-forward simulation on one thematic universe (N<=100) through February 2025; the validated object is reliability architecture, not transportable alpha.</description>

      <title>Growth versus equity in a stochastic multiplicative wealth model: The cost of redistribution and the emergence of an inequality Laffer curve</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27993</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.27993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A stochastic multiplicative wealth model with taxation and redistribution is extended to include two channels through which fiscal policy can reduce the economy's average growth rate: productive disincentive (a tax-dependent mean return) and administrative inefficiency (loss of part of the collected revenue). For uniform redistribution, the stationary density of normalized wealth remains an inverse-gamma law, but its shape parameter acquires a richer dependence on the tax rate. The central finding is the emergence of an "inequality Laffer curve": when the disincentive is sufficiently strong, the Gini coefficient first decreases, reaches a minimum at a finite tax rate, and then increases again as taxation intensifies. In the extreme limit the stationary state collapses back to the condensed phase, restoring the oligarchic transition. Both channels also create a direct trade-off between inequality and long-run average wealth, giving rise to a welfare-maximizing tax rate. The two channels are combined into a single analytically tractable model, and all predictions are validated by agent-based simulations. The results show that the qualitative existence of an optimal tax rate is robust whenever the aggregate growth rate responds to fiscal policy, while the inequality Laffer curve is a specific prediction of the productive-disincentive channel.</description>

      <title>Model Doubt, Risk Aversion, and the Threshold for Trading: A Geometry of Pricing Measures</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28288</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.28288v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much model doubt can an investor bear before they stop trading? Our investor treats every model within a given Kullback-Leibler divergence of their reference model as plausible. In a finite one-period market, they hold no risky asset exactly when this doubt reaches the smallest divergence of a pricing measure from their model, for every smooth, strictly increasing, strictly concave utility; non-traded claims then have intervals of no-trade prices. Below this threshold, for log utility and in a given market, doubt acts exactly like higher constant relative risk aversion; their robust pricing measure moves from the log-utility measure toward the pricing measure at that smallest divergence. With a century of U.S. data, a log investor who doubts the Black-Scholes mean return over its 95% confidence interval acts like a fully trusting investor with relative risk aversion of about 1.8 instead of 1. Implied doubt turns a quote into a radius; the mean VIX implies doubt beyond the threshold, but whether significantly so depends on the reference model. By a known identity, real-world, pricing, and share (stock-numeraire) measures form a triangle whose Pythagorean defect is a log risk premium; one side is half the squared (ideal) VIX times the horizon. Since 1990, the U.S. defect averages about 10% per year, about 1 point of it entropy premium.</description>

      <title>Echoes of the boom in hydraulic fracturing: What changes in Louisiana's energy complex reveal about global energy cycles</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28309</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.28309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The expansion of hydraulic fracturing (i.e. fracking) led to global shifts in energy markets that were felt acutely along the US Gulf Coast and particularly in the state of Louisiana. This article presents a data-focused examination of trends in the energy industry, and shows how they led to potentially counterintuitive, negative impacts in Louisiana's economy. Most notably, hydraulic fracturing led to a massive expansion in oil and gas supplies that contributed to a significant decline in oil prices in late 2014, contributing to significant job losses. Louisiana's economic downturns were tied to global shifts in energy markets that had major geostrategic implications. More broadly, results indicate that large and long period cycles in the supply, demand and price of oil can have widespread impacts on job creation and loss. In states like Louisiana with a large and diversified energy complex, the impacts of these trends can be highly uneven. One impact in the 21st Century appears to be highly concentrated areas of industrial development within a broader pattern of regional economic decline. Furthermore, trends identified in this study suggest the potential for the emergence of major cycles in the gas market. Whereas natural gas was previously mostly transported by pipelines and sold through long-term contracts, the emergence of liquified natural gas creates the potential for more volatile gas market dynamics. The implications of gas market cycles, while not yet known, could be of major economic significance.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Modeling Joint Tail Risk and Dependence for Cryptocurrencies via a Copula-Based Semiparametric Framework</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28524</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.28524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study proposes a Bayesian copula-based bivariate semiparametric framework for jointly forecasting Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) while modeling cross-asset tail dependence. The marginal dynamics are specified using four ES-CAViaR-type models, including extensions incorporating Rogers-Satchell and Garman-Klass volatility measures. To construct the copula inputs, we use the empirical ranks of standardized residuals, which depend on the marginal parameters, thereby linking marginal tail dynamics and dependence modeling without requiring fully specified marginal distributions. Clayton and BB1 copulas are considered, and adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are used for estimation and joint tail-risk forecasting. A simulation study under a DCC-GARCH-$t$ data-generating process evaluates the finite-sample forecasting performance of the proposed framework. Using Bitcoin and Ethereum data, we evaluate one-step-ahead forecasts from 2020 to 2025 through a rolling-window forecasting scheme and compare the proposed models with Bayesian DCC-GARCH-N and DCC-GARCH-$t$ benchmarks. Rolling copula estimates also reveal time-varying asymmetry in Bitcoin-Ethereum tail dependence, with lower-tail dependence remaining higher than upper-tail dependence for most of the period. The proposed framework delivers competitive forecasting performance for both marginal and joint tail risk.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Project financing in vanishing forests: Do investors care about nature protection?</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29281</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.29281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biodiversity risks are increasingly recognized by financial market participants, yet their measurement at the corporate-entity level obscures the locations and assets through which they arise. Project finance links identifiable physical assets to dedicated financing contracts, allowing us to examine this transmission more directly. By linking 9,037 project-loan pairs in 115 countries, we relate bank loan spreads to projects' proximity to protected areas, surrounding forest loss and lenders' nature policies. We find that lenders price proximity to protected areas only when they also have explicit nature risk policies and particularly within 1.5 km buffers from the project location. Realised forest loss around a project is priced more consistently than forest loss after the loan is signed, and risk pricing near protected areas strengthens after the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Listed company sponsors also experience negative, but short-lived, abnormal returns around loan signings for projects within 30 km of protected areas or in high-forest-loss landscapes. Our results suggest that while nature risk is partially priced in project finance, this is not a strong incentive to deter significant harm to nature.</description>

    <item>
      <title>What the annual energy balance hides: the coordination value of digital platforms for positive energy districts</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29485</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.29485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Positive energy districts (PEDs) are usually assessed by annual net energy, whereas distribution networks operate hour by hour. An annually positive district still imports on low-generation hours and exports or curtails on high-generation hours. How large this hourly imbalance is behind an annual balance, and how much of it coordination among prosumers can close without new physical capacity, is not established. This paper models a multi-carrier prosumer community coupling electricity and heat behind a shared grid connection with a net-export hosting limit. The model is solved as a centralized community problem and as a price-taking peer-to-peer (P2P) market. Under convexity, the equilibrium implements the regularized community optimum and the P2P and congestion prices are the duals of the pool-clearing and hosting constraints. The model is calibrated to six European district archetypes with constructed hourly profiles. Hourly self-sufficiency is only 48-50% in the four deeply studied districts and ranges from 48-55% across all six, leaving a no-platform coordination gap of 2.8-5.9% of no-platform economic cost. The shared-forecast step recovers only 6-18% of the gap, while grid-aware pricing reduces curtailment by 45% in the primary district. Coordination mainly reduces surplus-side inefficiency, whereas closing the deficit side requires storage. The results are scenario-based projections for calibrated archetypes, and the operating benefit is small and contingent on binding hosting limits and high feed-in remuneration. For regulators and distribution system operators this supports hourly, bidirectional indicators alongside the annual positive-energy target, and a congestion charge active only in binding hours with a predetermined refund, while the business case for a platform at district scale rests on grid-side value and aggregation across districts.</description>

    <item>
      <title>How to Mismatch Consumers</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29502</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.29502v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Should a platform show all consumers all products, or at least those they like most? Or could it raise consumer surplus by mismatching some consumers: showing them only less-preferred products or even excluding them from trade? I show that in both monopoly and duopoly, mismatching can raise aggregate consumer surplus by inducing lower prices. In duopoly, consumer-optimal matching uses a cutoff policy: along each diagonal of equal valuation differences, consumers with lower valuations are matched only to less-preferred products, and some may subsequently be excluded. With independent uniform valuations, this raises aggregate consumer surplus by about 41% over full matching.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Gated Payoff-Weighted Net Profit Maximization For Online Portfolio Selection With Transaction Costs</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29552</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.29552v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we study online portfolio selection (OLPS) problems. The net profit maximization (NPM) acting upon Adaptive Online Moving Average (AOLMA), namely the AOLNPM strategy in portfolio selection, trades when forecast gain exceeds the transaction cost. In essence, this method relies heavily on calibrated forecasts. Indeed, we show that AOLMA forecasts overstate the realized relative returns. We therefore design a gate that adjusts how strongly an AOLMA forecast is used; for each asset, it learns the recent mixture proportion assigned to AOLMA from predictive likelihoods against a neutral forecast (no change). The proportion therefore estimates the extent to which the forecast is realized. We then feed the resulting forecast into the NPM portfolio rule, where the gate acts as an asset-specific cost threshold. A payoff-weighted fund combines gated NPM experts with fixed decay factors in proportion to their wealth and needs no learning rate. On nine datasets with a transaction cost rate of 0.1%, our method produces 5.9 times the wealth of AOLNPM in geometric mean and sits above AOLNPM on every dataset, with its preponderance growing with the cost rate.</description>

      <title>Marked INAR model and the rough Hawkes--Heston limit</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29565</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.29565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop a discrete-time Monte Carlo algorithm for the rough Hawkes-Heston model based on a nearly unstable marked integer-valued autoregressive (INAR) process. We implement the algorithm with a block fast Fourier transform (FFT) scheme that evaluates the excitation convolution in $O(N\log^2 N)$ operations per path on an $N$-bin grid. We prove joint convergence in law of the spot variance, log price and common marked point measure to their rough Hawkes-Heston limits. We prove convergence of European call and put option prices, as well as convergence of arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices to their continuously monitored values. For European options, the one-year implied volatility smiles computed from the grid transform approach the continuous affine reference across four roughness levels. Monte Carlo experiments on the same three grids compare arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices with a finer-grid reference and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm.</description>

      <title>Neighbourhood flood damage amplifies mortgage default cascades</title>

      <description>arXiv:2611.30880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study online stochastic gradient descent for a single linear neuron in a teacher-student setting with Gaussian inputs of arbitrary covariance. Abstract: How do ancestral climate experiences shape today's attitudes towards environmental issues? Abstract: Artificial intelligence feels omnipresent, yet the disruption many expect has not fully arrived. The main reason is not model capability, nor even the tools built to harness those models. Abstract: We develop a mean field game (MFG) model for optimal trading in which the interaction among traders is mediated by the dynamics of the limit order book. Replacing the logarithmic score by another proper scoring rule changes both the target the filter tracks and the precision with which it tracks it. These filters form a subclass of the PRADA models of de Punder (2026), and we study their properties at the level of the filtered path.
  In an in-fill framework, the local tracking error is an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process. Optimised over the gain, its invariant variance is the geometric mean of the target's volatility and an effective observation noise determined by the scoring rule. Tracking efficiency is the squared correlation between the scoring-rule driver and the true score at the rule's own target. In scale models it equals the asymptotic relative efficiency of the corresponding static minimum-score estimator.
  The resulting frontier quantifies the robustness--efficiency trade-off. Under Gaussian innovations, density-power and CRPS volatility filters raise minimal tracking risk by 3% and 11%. Under Student-$t_5$ innovations, the Gaussian log-score filter raises it by 58% in the limit, and by more at daily frequency.
  We also give primitive conditions for bounded scale-invariant drivers, a matrix version, a population self-tuning result for the gain, minimum-score estimation theory whose invertibility conditions hold at the fitted values, and diffusion limits. An international equity application separates the roles of the predictive density and the scoring rule.</description>

      <title>Exponential Convergence of the Lifted Gradient Flow of the Bass Functional</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40404</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.40404v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: How quickly can we construct the martingale with prescribed initial and terminal laws that is closest to Brownian motion in the sense of the martingale Benamou-Brenier problem? The construction requires the initial law of an auxiliary Brownian motion. One can take this law to be the distribution of a minimizer of the lifted Bass functional. In dimension one, Backhoff, Pammer and Schachermayer proved, under additional assumptions, that the gradient flow of this functional converges exponentially to a minimizer.
  We extend this result to arbitrary dimension. Under the assumptions of the paper, the gradient flow starting from a bounded random vector converges exponentially in $L^2$ to the minimizer with the same mean. We prove this by showing that, for a fixed random vector $X$ with the prescribed initial law, the lifted Bass functional is strongly convex on each set of $\sigma(X)$-measurable vectors with a prescribed mean and a common $L^\infty$ bound.</description>

      <title>Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22033</link>
      <description>arXiv:2611.22033v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.</description>
